nameStory: The 'mountain' part of this honeysuckle's name hints at its preference for cooler, higher elevation spots in our region. 'Fly honeysuckle' refers to the way its paired berries dangle like little flies hanging from the branches, quite different from the tubular climbing vines most people think of as honeysuckles.
description: Mountain fly-honeysuckle is a low-growing, deciduous shrub that typically reaches 2-4 feet tall with an open, somewhat scraggly appearance. Unlike the familiar climbing honeysuckles with their fragrant tubular flowers, this native species produces small, paired yellowish flowers that develop into distinctive blue berries. It's a woodland shrub that prefers the cooler temperatures and acidic soils of northern New England's mountains and forests. The whole plant has a delicate, almost wispy quality compared to its more robust honeysuckle cousins.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Two blue berries fused together at their base, creating a distinctive 'double berry' that feels slightly soft and has a waxy surface when ripe in late summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, oval leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy (villous) on both surfaces, especially underneath - run your finger along the leaf and you'll notice the fine hairs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, pale yellow tubular flowers appear in pairs from the leaf joints in late spring, each about half an inch long and not particularly showy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading shrub with thin, somewhat arching branches that give it an open, airy appearance rather than a dense bushy look

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older stems develop a slightly shreddy, grayish bark that peels in thin strips

habitat: Look for mountain fly-honeysuckle in cool, moist woodlands, especially in mountainous areas of northern New England. It thrives in acidic soils under partial shade, often growing alongside blueberries, mountain laurel, and other acid-loving plants. You'll most commonly find it at higher elevations in mixed coniferous-deciduous forests.

seasonality.spring: Small paired yellowish flowers bloom in late May to early June, appearing from the leaf joints just as the soft, fuzzy leaves are fully emerging.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive paired blue berries ripen in July and August, standing out against the green foliage and providing the best identification feature.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to reddish before dropping, and some berries may persist into early autumn if not eaten by birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic opposite branching pattern, with small reddish-brown buds and slightly shreddy bark on older stems.

funFact: The paired berries of mountain fly-honeysuckle are actually two separate flowers that fused together as they developed - if you look closely at a ripe berry, you can sometimes still see the tiny remnants of both flower parts at the tip, like a botanical conjoined twin!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, swamp fly honeysuckle, but mountain fly-honeysuckle has noticeably hairier (more villous) leaves that feel fuzzy to the touch, while swamp fly honeysuckle's leaves are smooth. Remember: 'villosa' sounds like 'velvet' - both are soft and fuzzy!
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that not all honeysuckles are climbing vines - the fly honeysuckles are shrubs that represent some of our native honeysuckle species, quite different from the invasive Japanese honeysuckle that most people know. The scientific name 'villosa' means 'hairy' or 'shaggy,' referring to the soft fuzz on the leaves.
compareHints: Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats. Unlike the invasive honeysuckles (Japanese, Morrow's, Tatarian), it's a low shrub rather than a climbing vine or tall bush, and its berries are blue rather than red. The paired, fused berries immediately distinguish all fly honeysuckles from other members of the honeysuckle family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
